A stop here is a chance to discover a more intimate side of the city after its broad avenues. On days when the market is open, antiques and handmade crafts add to the scene; at other times, the main attractions are the old facades, trees, and café tables.

At Plaza Francia, you want to stop and gaze upward for a long time. Aconcagua's south face rises above the rocky valley: dark cliffs are cut by bands of snow, with hanging glaciers higher up. Against this backdrop, a person carrying a backpack looks tiny. People make the journey here to come close to a mountain that usually remains a distant summit on the horizon.

The route follows the Horcones Valley from Confluencia Camp in Aconcagua Park, in Argentina's Mendoza Province. On trekking itineraries, the name Plaza Francia often refers to the walk to a viewpoint below the south face. The exposed high-altitude trail and cold wind make it a genuine mountain day, even when a technical ascent is not planned.

On the Ada Tours expedition, this hike serves as acclimatization before the journey to Plaza de Mulas. After stopping at the foot of the face, the group returns to Confluencia for the night. The trip requires suitable physical fitness and a permit for the selected park itinerary; the guide determines the final route according to the weather and participants' condition.

The square brings together open space, green areas, and the facades of historic buildings. From here, a city walk continues through the streets of old Lima, including to the Santo Domingo Monastery.

Exploring the square and visiting the buildings around it are separate parts of an itinerary. Entry to the cathedral or other monuments depends on opening schedules and the specific excursion's inclusions.

In the shade of large trees, the square feels like a small park amid the surrounding city buildings. You can linger by the monument to General San Martín, stroll along the paths, and see how this green space fits into the urban setting.

The site's history is connected with the formation of the Mounted Grenadiers Regiment in 1812. The square was later named after San Martín, and landscape architect Carlos Thays contributed to its design. The variety of trees and monuments makes it an interesting stop both for learning about history and for a short rest.

The square is included in sightseeing routes around Argentina's capital. It is easy to combine with the city's other squares and avenues while leaving time for a walk beneath the trees.
